concepts.name: Article 21: Original vs. Expanded Scope
key_dimensions: Original narrow reading in A.K. Gopalan (1950): 'procedure established by law' vs. 'due process of law'
Landmark shift in Maneka Gandhi (1978): procedure must be fair, just, and reasonable
Distinction between Indian 'procedure established by law' and American 'due process' clause
UPSC trap: Article 21 protects citizens AND non-citizens (all persons), unlike Article 19

concepts.name: Right to Life vs. Right to Mere Animal Existence
key_dimensions: Francis Coralie Mullin (1981): right to life includes right to live with dignity, not just physical survival
Expansion to include livelihood, health, shelter, and education under Article 21
Olga Tellis (1985): right to livelihood as part of right to life — eviction of pavement dwellers
UPSC trap: right to livelihood is not absolute; it can be restricted by fair procedure

concepts.name: Right to Privacy as a Fundamental Right
key_dimensions: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017): 9-judge bench unanimously held privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21
Overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) which had denied privacy as FR
Three-fold test for restricting privacy: legality, legitimate aim, proportionality
UPSC trap: Privacy is not enumerated in the Constitution; it is a judicially evolved right — implications for data protection legislation

concepts.name: Right to Health and Medical Care
key_dimensions: Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996): state obligated to provide emergency medical care
Consumer Education & Research Centre (1995): right to health in workplace as part of Article 21
Intersection with DPSP Article 47 (duty of state to raise nutrition levels and public health)
UPSC trap: Article 21 makes health a justiciable right even though Article 47 is non-justiciable

concepts.name: Right to Education Under Article 21
key_dimensions: Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993): right to education derived from Article 21
Subsequently codified as Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002): free and compulsory education for 6-14 years
UPSC trap: Article 21A covers only 6–14 age group; Article 21 (judicial interpretation) had a broader scope
RTE Act 2009 as the legislative arm of Article 21A; distinction between Article 21 and 21A in enforcement

concepts.name: Right Against Solitary Confinement and Handcuffing
key_dimensions: Sunil Batra (1978 & 1980): solitary confinement violates Article 21 unless exceptional circumstances exist
Prem Shankar Shukla (1980): handcuffing prisoners violates right to dignity under Article 21
Supreme Court guidelines on when handcuffing is permissible (compelling circumstances + judicial order)
UPSC trap: these rights apply even to convicted prisoners — Article 21 does not cease upon conviction

concepts.name: Right to Speedy Trial
key_dimensions: Hussainara Khatoon (1979): prolonged detention of undertrial prisoners violates Article 21
Abdul Rehman Antulay (1992): speedy trial is an essential component of Article 21
Distinction: no fixed constitutional timeline; it is assessed case-by-case (unlike the US Sixth Amendment)
UPSC trap: right to speedy trial is not explicitly in Constitution; it is judge-made — relevant for prelims MCQs on 'which article'

concepts.name: Right to Legal Aid and Fair Trial
key_dimensions: Hussainara Khatoon: state duty to provide free legal aid to indigent accused
M.H. Hoskot (1978): right to free legal services as part of fair, just, and reasonable procedure under Article 21
Constitutional backing also from Article 39A (DPSP) — again making a non-justiciable DPSP enforceable via Article 21
UPSC trap: Article 39A is a DPSP, but its substance is enforced as FR via Article 21 — classic overlap question

concepts.name: Right Against Custodial Violence and Torture
key_dimensions: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997): landmark guidelines on arrest, detention, and custodial rights
Nilabati Behera (1993): state liable to pay compensation for custodial death — public law remedy distinct from private law
India's non-ratification of UN Convention Against Torture — judicial gap-filling via Article 21
UPSC trap: D.K. Basu guidelines are not statute; they are Supreme Court directives under Article 32/142 — legislative status question

concepts.name: Right to Die / Euthanasia and Article 21
key_dimensions: P. Rathinam (1994): right to die included in right to life — struck down Section 309 IPC
Gian Kaur (1996): 5-judge bench overruled P. Rathinam — right to life does not include right to die
Common Cause v. Union of India (2018): passive euthanasia and 'living will' permitted under Article 21 with safeguards
UPSC trap: active euthanasia is still illegal; passive euthanasia with advance directive is permissible — critical distinction

concepts.name: Right to Clean Environment as Part of Article 21
key_dimensions: Subhash Kumar (1991): right to pollution-free water and air is part of right to life
M.C. Mehta cases: series of judgments linking environmental protection to Article 21
Intersection with Article 48A (DPSP: environment protection) and Article 51A(g) (Fundamental Duty)
UPSC trap: environment protection is simultaneously a FR (via Art. 21), DPSP (Art. 48A), and FD (Art. 51A-g) — unique triple overlap

concepts.name: Right to Shelter and Housing
key_dimensions: Chameli Singh (1996): right to shelter is a fundamental right under Article 21 read with Articles 19(1)(e) and 17
Olga Tellis: prior notice and alternative shelter required before eviction of slum dwellers
Distinction from absolute right: state can evict for legitimate public purpose with fair procedure
UPSC trap: right to shelter is not an absolute right to government-provided housing — it is a right against arbitrary eviction

concepts.name: Right to Food and Nutrition
key_dimensions: PUCL v. Union of India (2001 — ongoing): Supreme Court orders on mid-day meals and food schemes treated as Article 21 obligations
Linking Article 21 to food security schemes (PDS, ICDS, mid-day meal) — judicial activism in socio-economic rights
National Food Security Act 2013 as statutory backing — relationship between judicial direction and legislative action
UPSC trap: right to food is not explicitly in Article 21 text; it is derived — often tested as 'which right is NOT explicitly mentioned'

concepts.name: Right to Reputation and Dignity
key_dimensions: Umesh Kumar (2013): right to reputation is part of right to life under Article 21
Tension between Article 21 (reputation/dignity) and Article 19(1)(a) (freedom of speech) — balancing test
Constitutional validity of criminal defamation (Section 499/500 IPC) upheld in Subramanian Swamy (2016)
UPSC trap: criminal defamation survives constitutional challenge because protecting reputation = protecting Article 21

concepts.name: Rights of Prisoners Under Article 21
key_dimensions: Charles Sobhraj (1978): prisoners retain all fundamental rights except those taken away by lawful incarceration
Right to basic amenities, medical care, reading material, and family visits in prison
Distinction between undertrial prisoners (presumption of innocence + stronger rights) vs. convicted prisoners
UPSC trap: Article 21 does NOT suspend for prisoners — common misconception; only restrictions directly necessitated by imprisonment are valid

concepts.name: Article 21 and Capital Punishment
key_dimensions: Bachan Singh (1980): death penalty upheld as constitutional but restricted to 'rarest of rare' cases
Machhi Singh (1983): guidelines for determining 'rarest of rare' (nature of crime, manner, motive, magnitude)
Delay in execution as violation of Article 21: Shattrughan Chauhan (2014) — inordinate delay = commutation of death sentence
UPSC trap: death penalty is NOT per se unconstitutional under Article 21 — the procedure must be just and fair

concepts.name: Right to Know / Right to Information Under Article 21
key_dimensions: S.P. Gupta (1981): right to know about government functioning derived from Articles 19(1)(a) and 21
Reliance Petrochemicals (1988): right to know as part of right to life — access to information for informed citizenship
RTI Act 2005 as statutory recognition — relationship between judicial FR and legislative enactment
UPSC trap: RTI Act has exceptions (Sections 8 & 9); these are valid restrictions on the judicially-evolved right to know

concepts.name: Maneka Gandhi Doctrine: Inter-linking of Fundamental Rights
key_dimensions: Maneka Gandhi (1978): Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not watertight compartments — a law must satisfy ALL three simultaneously
'Golden Triangle' of Articles 14 (equality), 19 (freedoms), and 21 (life/liberty) — any law curtailing Article 21 must pass tests of all three
Shift from Gopalan's 'specific entry' theory to holistic reading of Part III
UPSC trap: the 'golden triangle' is judge-made doctrine, not constitutional text — frequently tested in context of which case established it

concepts.name: Article 21 During National Emergency
key_dimensions: ADM Jabalpur (1976 — the Habeas Corpus case): majority held Article 21 can be suspended during Emergency — darkest hour of SC
44th Amendment (1978): amended Article 359 to ensure Articles 20 and 21 CANNOT be suspended even during Emergency
Overruling of ADM Jabalpur in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017): Justice D.Y. Chandrachud explicitly called it wrongly decided
UPSC trap: Post-44th Amendment, Article 21 is the ONLY Fundamental Right (along with Art. 20) that cannot be suspended during Emergency — critical 'only' clause

concepts.name: Horizontal Application of Article 21: State vs. Private Actors
key_dimensions: Article 21 traditionally enforceable only against 'State' as defined in Article 12
Vishaka (1997): sexual harassment guidelines binding on private employers — indirect horizontal effect via Article 21
MC Mehta (gas leak): private industries can be held liable for violating Article 21 through 'absolute liability' doctrine
UPSC trap: Article 21 is directly vertical (against State), but courts have extended obligations to private bodies performing public functions — nuanced distinction
